about.title: About the data
about.lead: World Pulse turns published statistics into rates per second and places them on the globe. This page explains how, and where every number comes from.
about.honesty: Numbers are never invented. Every value carries a source, a data year and a confidence level. Most datasets are downloaded from the original publishers (World Bank, UN, WHO, Global Carbon Project, Ember, FAO, IEA, USGS…) by a reproducible script; the rest are transcribed from the cited reports. Check the original source before citing a figure.

method.title: Methodology
method.rates: Annual flows are converted into per-second rates using the mean Gregorian year (365.2425 days). Stocks, such as pupils, hospital beds and land area, remain levels and do not accumulate over time.
method.derived: Some counts are estimates calculated from a published percentage or density and its matching denominator in the same country and year. Each dataset states the formula and sources. These world figures are sums of available country estimates; missing countries are not assigned values by proxy. Different metrics can overlap and must not be added together.
method.years: For a given year the engine uses the exact data point; otherwise it interpolates linearly between the nearest years; beyond the series it carries the nearest value for a limited number of years (scaled by world growth when possible) and flags it as carried forward. It never extrapolates further.
method.allocation: When only a world total exists, the part not covered by countries is either spread over the remaining countries by a declared proxy (population, GDP, internet users or land area) and marked as allocated — hatched on the map — or left unallocated.
method.coverage: Coverage is the share of the world total backed by country-level data.
method.profiles: Some activities follow the clock (emails, solar power). Their rate is modulated by each country’s local hour with a stylized daily curve whose average is 1, so daily totals are unchanged.
method.counters: Counters are computed from absolute timestamps (rate × elapsed time), never by adding per-frame steps, so they do not drift.
method.colours: Map colours use quantile classes: each colour groups about the same number of countries, so neighbours stay distinguishable even when a few countries dominate. The legend shows the range of every class.
method.centroids: Spikes stand at the centre of the largest land mass of each country; for 27 large countries an approximate population centre is used instead.
method.etl: Incomplete world-series releases are dropped by the data pipeline instead of being shown as a false decline. The additional datasets also check country coverage for reported world totals. Their country-only and derived series retain sparse national observations, with coverage and provenance shown explicitly.

limits.title: Known limitations
items: Official statistics are rounded to 4 significant figures and the most recent years are often provisional; the latest available year is used and shown.
Company statements (Google, OpenAI, YouTube, WhatsApp, Coca-Cola, McDonald’s) are self-reported and often lower bounds.
Allocation by proxy is a visual approximation, not a measurement of the receiving country.
Energy conversions (oil in barrels, gas in cubic metres) use standard average factors.

Poverty and service-access counts are derived estimates, not censuses. Undernourishment values reported as 2.5% may mean below 2.5%. Displacement counts measure incidents, so one person can be counted more than once.
Each country uses a single representative time zone; daily activity curves are stylized.
Disputed territories are drawn but carry no data (Kosovo excepted, following the World Bank).

tech.title: How it is built
tech.text: Angular 21 (signals, zoneless), Three.js with custom shaders, Natural Earth geometry. Everything is served from this site: no external APIs, no trackers.
